teaching.task: # HMS Year 11 V21 (The body and mind in motion): self-regulation and behaviour change. Most people intend to exercise more, so why do so many fail to change, and what actually closes the gap? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Knowing exercise is good isn't the problem. Almost everyone knows, which is why information campaigns change so little. Even intending isn't enough. In exercise studies, close to half of the people who intend to exercise don't follow through. Three things sit in the gap. The decision gets reopened every day, and each time is a chance to lose. The costs are today, and the benefits are years away. And nothing reminds you. That's why self-regulation matters: setting your own goals, checking what you actually do, and adjusting. It runs in three phases: set, monitor, evaluate. Set comes first, and the kind of goal matters more than its size. An outcome goal is a result, like winning the district final. It depends on opponents and luck, so you can do everything right and still miss it. A performance goal is a personal standard, like five kilometres in under twenty-five minutes. A process goal is an action you fully control, like three runs this week. That's the one that changes behaviour. Only you can fail it, and it gives you a win every week, which feeds competence. Make it specific, measurable, reachable but challenging, and time-bound. Then make it concrete. An implementation intention names when, where and how. That's B's fridge note, and it fixes all three problems. The decision is made once, on a calm day, so Tuesday at seven isn't a choice any more. The time and place become the cue. And there's nothing left to plan on the day. Stronger still, hook it onto something that already happens: I get off the bus two stops early and walk the rest. And A's advantages? Motivation forms the intention, but it doesn't get you out the door on a cold morning, and new shoes can feel like starting without being it.

scenes.teachingReason: Phase two is self-monitoring: recording what you actually did. Memory flatters us. People remember more sessions than their records show. And just recording a behaviour tends to change it, because a gap you can see is hard to ignore. Phase three is self-evaluation: comparing what you did with the plan, and deciding what it means. This is where most attempts die. Take one missed week. One person says, I missed three sessions because I've got no discipline. That attribution, the reason you give yourself, is personal and permanent, so next week looks hopeless, and she stops. Another says, I missed them because it was exam week. That's specific and temporary, so she starts again. Same week, opposite futures. And if a cause really is permanent, change the plan, not the person.

scenes.teachingReason: Self-regulation isn't only about turning up. It's a performance skill too. A self-regulating athlete sets her own goal for each session, watches her own execution, judges it honestly, and adjusts. That's the error detection of the autonomous stage, and the reason good coaches fade their feedback. An athlete who can't self-regulate improves only while the coach is watching. One who can improves in every hour she trains.

scenes.teachingReason: It has no plan for a lapse. The first sick day resets the count to zero, so one miss reads as total failure, and that's when people quit. The classic mistake is thinking specific means safe.
